item.title: CVE-2026-6471 Enables PostgreSQL Replication Accounts to Execute Arbitrary Code
item.content:encoded:
Window: 01 Sep 22:00 → 02 Sep 02:00 UTC (4 hours)

PostGREShell: The database powering much of the internet had an open door for 12 years — Must Read

Cyera researchers found a critical PostgreSQL flaw, CVE-2026-6471, that lets low-privilege replication accounts load arbitrary plugins and gain remote code execution, superuser access, and persistence. Organizations should patch immediately, audit replication accounts, and restrict replication access and outbound SMB/NFS traffic.

  • Cyera Research discovered CVE-2026-6471, a critical PostgreSQL vulnerability affecting every PostgreSQL version from 9.4 through 18.
  • The flaw lets an account with the REPLICATION attribute load and execute arbitrary code through the logical replication output plugin path because the plugin name is passed to the loader without validation.
  • On Windows, an attacker can exploit the issue remotely by using a UNC path over SMB so PostgreSQL loads a DLL from the attacker’s server without placing a file on the target system.
  • After code execution, the attacker can escalate to PostgreSQL superuser by calling internal functions and directly modifying pg_authid, bypassing normal SQL permission checks.
  • The article recommends applying the PostgreSQL security update, auditing REPLICATION accounts, restricting replication access in pg_hba.conf, and blocking outbound SMB and NFS from database servers.

Technologies: database

item.title: Healthcare Sharing, UK OT Proof, Snowflake Controls, and Self-Spoofed Phishing
item.content:encoded:
Window: 01 Sep 10:00 → 01 Sep 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

The Email From Yourself That Your Own Domain Disowned — May Read

A phishing email spoofed a financial advisor’s own address and reached the inbox despite SPF, DKIM, and DMARC failures because enforcement and composite authentication did not block it. The lure used a legitimate monday.com tracking link to redirect to a disposable credential-harvesting page, highlighting the need to flag self-addressed spoofing and inspect final link destinations.

  • A client-facing financial advisor received a document-signature phishing email whose From and To headers were both the advisor’s own work address.
  • The email arrived from commodity bulk-hosting infrastructure, explicitly failed SPF, had no DKIM signature, failed DMARC, yet Microsoft composite authentication returned a pass.
  • The “Start signing” button routed through a legitimate monday.com link-tracking hostname whose embedded token decoded to a disposable credential-harvesting page on sharedfile.realestatecotblrp.vu.
  • IRONSCALES Themis scored the message at 90% confidence and labeled it credential theft based on the suspicious link and the sender pattern of an external sender using an internal-looking self-addressed email.
  • The article recommends alerting on inbound mail where the From address matches the receiving mailbox, enforcing DMARC, watching for disagreement between authentication results, and resolving vendor link trackers before trusting them.

Technologies: email-security

Products: monday-com-link-tracker, themis, ironscales-adaptive-ai

Vendors: microsoft, monday-com, ironscales, colocrossing

What the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill’s New Standard of Proof Means for OT Organisations — Optional

The UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would push OT organisations from periodic compliance evidence to continuous, defensible proof that they know their assets, risks, ownership, and changes in real time. Many OT environments lack that live visibility today, so boards should close the gap before regulators or incidents force the issue.

  • The UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, as currently drafted, introduces a requirement for organisations to show ongoing proof that they manage cyber risk in their plants rather than relying on reasonable periodic effort.
  • The article says policies, point-in-time audits, named risk owners, and older penetration test reports will not be enough to answer regulator questions about what is connected to the network today, what has changed, or what current risk looks like.
  • OT environments are described as harder to manage continuously than IT environments because they often accumulate equipment over decades, include vendor-installed remote access, and have network changes made to maintain operations without formal records.
  • A defensible response requires a current asset inventory, risk scoring tied to operational function, mapping to a recognised methodology such as IEC 62443’s zone and conduit model, and clear ownership with a defined review cadence.
  • The article argues that many boards have not yet tested the gap between believing OT risk is managed and being able to prove it, and that closing this gap before a regulatory conversation is stronger than doing so during one.

item.title: Mirage Kitten Deploys NodeRabbit and PollCat RATs Against MEA Aviation and FinTech
item.content:encoded:
Window: 01 Sep 06:00 → 01 Sep 10:00 UTC (4 hours)

Mirage Kitten targeting aviation and FinTech sectors across the Middle East and Africa with a new malware set — Must Read

Kaspersky reports that Mirage Kitten is targeting aviation and fintech organizations in the Middle East and Africa with new cross-platform Node.js/JavaScript RATs called NodeRabbit and PollCat, delivered through fake recruiter coding challenges. The campaign marks a shift in the group’s tooling while continuing its use of LinkedIn lures, cloud-hosted infrastructure, and developer-focused social engineering.

  • Kaspersky uncovered two previously undocumented cross-platform RAT families, NodeRabbit and PollCat, during monitoring of Mirage Kitten activity.
  • Mirage Kitten delivered NodeRabbit and PollCat through spear-phishing messages on LinkedIn and other job search platforms that contained trojanized coding challenge archives.
  • NodeRabbit is built with Node.js, targets Windows, Linux, and macOS, and was observed in variants on systems in Afghanistan, Egypt, and Ethiopia.
  • PollCat is written in obfuscated JavaScript, starts during the fake React coding challenge application startup, and can continue running even if the user fails OTP validation.
  • Kaspersky attributes the activity to Mirage Kitten with high confidence based on malware similarities to Retrograde/MiniFast, victimology, lure-hosting tradecraft, and infrastructure patterns.

Technologies: cloud-platform, object-storage, package-registry, source-control, operating-system, proxy, remote-access

Products: node.js, azure-websites, amazon-s3, linkedin, npm, visual-studio-code, git, outlook, react, vite, express, windows, linux, macos

item.title: Anubis Hits Fairlife; pnpm 12 Rust Rewrite Adds Supply Chain Controls
item.content:encoded:
Window: 01 Sep 02:00 → 01 Sep 06:00 UTC (4 hours)

From a Stolen Login to a Ransomware Leak Site: What Our Telemetry Shows About the Path Threat Actors Take — Should Read

Constella links Fairlife’s public Anubis ransomware leak to a broader pattern where stolen credentials from infostealer-infected vendor laptops can give attackers access to corporate CMS, cloud, SSO, and internal systems. The key takeaway is that third-party credential exposure, including cookies and browser autofill data, must be monitored as seriously as a company’s own endpoints because it can become the first step toward ransomware.

  • Anubis added Fairlife, a dairy brand owned by The Coca-Cola Company, to its dark web extortion portal, and Coca-Cola publicly confirmed the ransomware incident.
  • Anubis claimed it exfiltrated close to a terabyte of internal data and used an optional wipe mode against part of the victim’s virtualization infrastructure.
  • The leaked data was organized into engineering and OT documentation, production and formulation data, and HR and people data.
  • Constella analyzed a separate credential package believed to belong to a third-party digital agency employee that contained 789 saved credential pairs, 540 browser session cookies, and a local password manager vault store.
  • The credential package included hundreds of credentials for brand site content management environments, plus credentials for cloud infrastructure, DevOps, source control, corporate identity, and SSO providers.

Technologies: cms, cloud-platform

Products: hunter-plus, adobe-experience-manager, crxde-lite, package-manager, amazon-web-services, slack

Vendors: constella, adobe, amazon-web-services, slack

pnpm 12’s Rust Rewrite Cuts Install Times by Up to 90% — May Read

pnpm 12 is now stable with a Rust rewrite that keeps pnpm 11 compatibility while delivering major install-time and storage improvements in early real-world testing. Its maintainers have narrowed public benchmark claims after flawed cross-package-manager comparisons, emphasizing faster pnpm performance rather than claiming overall market leadership.

  • pnpm 12 is now stable and replaces pnpm’s Node.js and TypeScript foundation with a Rust rewrite while preserving the commands, settings, and lockfile format used by pnpm 11.
  • In Vercel’s 21-project Turborepo workspace, pnpm 12 reduced median install times by 64.4% to 90.5% compared with pnpm 10.28 across six tested scenarios.
  • pnpm removed Bun and Yarn from the comparison displayed on its benchmark page after bugs made published cross-tool package manager rankings unreliable.
  • pnpm 12 adds supply chain security-related features including project-aware global bins, direct package manager provisioning, registry revisions, signed remote build artifacts, and deterministic cyclic lockfiles.
  • The upgrade has behavioral changes that may affect workflows, including removal of `pnpm install --resolution-only`, canonical HTTPS resolution for Git dependencies on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket, and warnings for unknown settings in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`.

Technologies: source-control

Products: pnpm, pnpm-12, pnpm-11, turborepo, bun, yarn, npm, corepack, node.js, deno, vlt-benchmark-suite, pnpr, github, gitlab, bitbucket

Vendors: pnpm, vercel, bun, yarn, npm, nodejs, deno, vlt, github, gitlab, bitbucket

So Your CFO's Phone Has Been Pwned: A DFIR Journey — Optional

When a CFO’s phone is suspected of compromise, a single IOC like an IP address should be treated as the start of a broader DFIR investigation, not the incident itself. Historical infrastructure data from tools like Censys can reveal malware panels, exploit chains, related hosts, and rotating attacker infrastructure needed to scope exposure and improve detections.

  • The article presents two fictional mobile incident response scenarios involving a CFO’s phone, one using Android malware resembling ERMAC or HookBot and one involving an iPhone connection to DarkSword infrastructure.
  • In the Android scenario, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint detects a sideloaded malicious APK called “Chrome Update,” prompting actions such as blocking the device from corporate resources, revoking sessions, preserving the phone, and reviewing accessible credentials.
  • Censys ARC observed the Android-related host 118.107.45[.]29 carrying a HookBot threat label from mid-July through August 13, 2026, and later changes matched HookBot’s IP-whitelist security gate behavior.
  • In the iPhone scenario, Zscaler web logs show the managed iPhone connected to 103.106.190[.]217, which Censys ARC observed serving an Apple ID credential-harvesting page alongside DarkSword iOS exploit-chain infrastructure.
  • The article emphasizes that an IP address, domain, certificate, or hash is evidence of a larger infrastructure picture, and that historical Internet data can help responders scope related hosts, prior activity, and future detections.

item.title: Malicious Packagist Themes Deliver iOS Spyware; Varonis Warns SIEM Insufficient for Databases
item.content:encoded:
Window: 31 Aug 14:00 → 31 Aug 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

13 Malicious Packagist Themes Deliver iOS Spyware That Steals Crypto Wallet Seeds — Must Read

Socket researchers found 13 malicious Packagist Composer themes for Vietnamese streaming CMS sites that inject JavaScript to run ad-fraud redirects and, on vulnerable iPhones, a FUNNULL-hosted exploit chain that installs spyware. The payload can steal sensitive iOS data including keychain contents, messages, photos, location history, and crypto wallet seeds, so affected site operators should remove the packages and users should update iOS immediately.

  • Socket’s Threat Research Team found 13 malicious Composer theme packages on Packagist across five vendor namespaces that inject JavaScript into Vietnamese movie and comic streaming sites that install them.
  • The injected JavaScript runs a mobile ad-fraud and gambling-redirect chain, and on iPhones it can trigger a WebKit-to-kernel exploit chain that installs spyware.
  • Apple confirmed that the kernel escape used by the iOS chain was already fixed in iOS and macOS 26.1 before Socket’s report, while the two WebKit entry points are public and listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
  • The spyware payload can collect keychain databases, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS, address book, Photos, browser cookies, call history, location history, account databases, and crypto-wallet seed or mnemonic data from several wallet apps.
  • The article recommends that site operators remove any themes from the vsmov, vsphim, haiau009, chilltvcms, or ophimcms vendors, rotate credentials handled on the host, inspect theme scripts, and block the listed network indicators.

Technologies: package-registry, cms, mobile-os, operating-system, browser

item.title: JSCeal Deobfuscation, Next.js CVE-2026-75604, PaperCut Exploitation, and ValleyRAT Campaigns
item.content:encoded:
Window: 31 Aug 10:00 → 31 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-75604) Next.js Remote Code Execution via Windows Path Traversal — Should Read

A critical Next.js flaw, CVE-2026-75604, can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on self-hosted Windows deployments using affected versions and routing/cache configurations. Organizations should urgently identify Windows-hosted Next.js apps and upgrade to the fixed releases, as there is no reliable workaround.

  • CVE-2026-75604 is a critical path traversal flaw in Next.js that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to write files outside the framework’s cache directory and reach remote code execution on the host.
  • The vulnerability affects Next.js 13.4 up to 15.5.24 and 16.0 up to 16.3.3 when the application runs on a Windows filesystem and uses the Pages Router or the App Router without Cache Components.
  • Linux and macOS deployments are not affected, and applications running on Vercel’s managed platform are not affected because that infrastructure runs on Linux.
  • Vercel released fixed versions in Next.js 15.5.24 and 16.3.3, and the article states there is no known workaround for affected Windows-hosted applications.
  • The article recommends inventorying Windows-hosted Next.js deployments, confirming pinned Next.js versions, monitoring cache paths, blocking percent-encoded backslash sequences, and auditing externally reachable incremental static regeneration routes until patching is confirmed.

Technologies: operating-system, web-server

Products: next-js, cycognito-platform, windows-server, iis, libheif

Vendors: vercel, cycognito, microsoft, libheif-project

ValleyRAT masquerading as adware — Should Read

Kaspersky found that attackers are disguising the ValleyRAT backdoor as signed QN Wallpaper adware, using DLL sideloading to disable defenses, persist, steal keystrokes and clipboard data, and download additional payloads. The campaign is likely linked to Silver Fox and has mainly affected users in China and India.

  • Kaspersky analyzed an installer initially classified as adware and found that it triggered an infection chain delivering the ValleyRAT backdoor instead of functioning as advertising software.
  • The installer deployed a modified version of the Chinese QN Wallpaper desktop wallpaper tool and used a malicious libcef.dll for DLL sideloading under the guise of a signed process.
  • The malicious libcef.dll decrypted and loaded AES-encrypted ValleyRAT payloads from either the PeLoader file or its own resources, depending on whether it was running inside QnWallpaper.exe or QnwPlayer.exe.
  • ValleyRAT can log keystrokes, capture clipboard contents, collect system information, take screenshots, update C2 addresses, download additional modules, and reboot or shut down the computer on command.
  • Kaspersky detected ValleyRAT and associated malware more than 100,000 times in 2026, affecting more than 1,500 unique users primarily in China and India, and attributed the campaign as likely linked to Silver Fox.

Technologies: antivirus, operating-system

Products: qn-wallpaper, windows-defender, windows

Vendors: kaspersky, keansoft, microsoft

Breaking the Seal: Static Deobfuscation of JSCeal’s Compiled V8 Bytecode — Should Read

Check Point researchers built and released a fully static pipeline to deobfuscate JSCeal’s compiled V8 bytecode payloads, turning heavily obfuscated Node.js malware into analyzable pseudocode without executing it. The recovered code shows JSCeal is a broad crypto-focused stealer with browser credential theft, keylogging, screenshots, Telegram theft, and local HTTPS interception capabilities.

  • Check Point Research has tracked JSCeal since early 2025 as a cryptocurrency-focused stealer delivered as compiled V8 bytecode and executed by a bundled Node.js runtime.
  • The analyzed JSCeal payloads were protected with javascript-obfuscator techniques including RC4-protected strings, control-flow flattening, proxy functions, and operation wrappers.
  • Check Point Research developed and released a fully static deobfuscation toolkit that transforms View8 pseudocode without executing the malware.
  • The deobfuscated output exposed JSCeal capabilities including browser credential theft, keylogging, screenshot capture, Telegram session theft, cryptocurrency-focused collection, and HTTPS traffic interception through a local proxy.
  • More recent JSCeal developments include V8 code caches generated for a newer Node.js and V8 version, an AES-256-CBC payload-encryption layer, and macOS targeting.

Technologies: operating-system, browser, proxy

Products: jsceal, jsc-deobfuscator, view8, v8, node.js, javascript-obfuscator, brotli, puppeteer, puppeteer-extra, ghost-cursor, macos, windows

Vendors: check-point, google, nodejs, javascript-obfuscator, view8, hasherezade, microsoft

One Target List, Six Weeks of Conference Invites — Should Read

A patient phishing operator used an aged, properly authenticated attacker-owned domain to repeatedly target named employees at one pharmaceutical CDMO with personalized conference-invitation emails carrying a malicious PDF. The key lesson is that SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain age, and sender familiarity can all look normal, so defenders need payload analysis and per-recipient behavioral detection to catch these campaigns.

  • On July 9, 2026, a senior commercial leader at a pharmaceutical contract development and manufacturing organization received a personalized industry-summit invitation with a malicious brochure PDF attached.
  • Six weeks later, on August 20, 2026, four more individually named mailboxes at the same organization were targeted with similar personalized conference invitations and matching brochure attachments.
  • The emails passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication because the attacker owned and correctly configured the sending domain.
  • The attacker’s sending domain, nexora-summits[.]com, was created on December 5, 2025, making it roughly seven months old at the first recorded send.
  • The attachment scanner returned a malicious verdict on the PDF, and Themis scored the message at 90 percent confidence before mitigating it across the affected mailboxes.

Technologies: email-security

Products: themis

Vendors: ironscales, microsoft

  • McKesson disclosed a data breach involving unauthorized access to third-party applications and data theft, and ShinyHunters claimed it exfiltrated about 1TB of data containing approximately 284 million patient-related records.

  • U.S. authorities announced the disruption of QScan and QTRouter, two platforms operated by the China-linked group QTFY to target U.S. critical infrastructure and government networks.
